texts.facts: 1 (a) Detailed Accident Report (hereinafter referred as DAR) filed is being treated as Claim Petition under Section 166 (1) read with Section 166 (4) MV Act. It pertains to alleged accident of Shankar (hereinafter referred as claimant) by offending vehicle bearing Registration No. DL 3SEH 2152, being driven by Sh. Shankar Kumar (hereinafter referred as R-1), owned by Sh. Akash Kumar, (hereinafter referred as R-2) and insured with The Oriental Insurance Company Limited (hereinafter referred as R-3). 2. BRIEF FACTS (a) Preliminary information regarding the accident in question was received at PS Lajpat Nagar vide GD No. 3A dated 03.06.2020 from AIIMS Trauma Center concerning the MLC of the injured person. Upon receipt of the said information, the Investigating Officer (IO) proceeded to AIIMS Trauma Center and collected the MLC of the injured Shankar, which contained the description of road traffic accident noted by doctor. The IO also obtained the MLC of the respondent no. 1/driver of the offending vehicle; however, the doctor opined that he was not fit for giving a statement at that time. Thereafter, the IO visited the residence of the injured, where the injured narrated the facts of the accident and submitted a written complaint. In his complaint, the injured stated that on 02.06.2020 at about 09:30 PM, he had MACT No. 01/2021 Shankar Vs Deepak & Ors. Page No. 2 of 27 (rpt) gone to Nehru Nagar and on returning from Nehur Nagar, while he was crossing the road near the bus stand, a motorcyclist riding his motorcycle bearing registration no. DL-3SEH-2152 (make KTM, colour orange) in speedy and reckless manner, came from the Lajpat Nagar side and forcefully struck him. Due to the impact, both the injured and the motorcyclist fell onto the road, and the injured sustained multiple injuries on different part of his body. In the meantime, one Kunal, known to the injured (living in jhuggis near the spot of accident) reached the spot and shifted the injured to AIIMS Trauma Center in an auto -rickshaw. It was further stated that the motorcyclist was also admitted to AIIMS Trauma Center. The accident was stated to have occurred due to the rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle. (b) On the basis of the statement of the injured and the contents of the MLC, an FIR was registered under the relevant provisions of law. Notice under Section 133 of the Motor Vehicles Act was served upon the owner of the offending vehicle, namely Akash, who responded to such notice that on 02.06.2020, his brother Deepak was driving the said vehicle. The documents of the offending vehicle were seized and verified from the concerned authority. Mechanical Inspection of offending vehicle was also conducted. Driver / R-1 disclosed that he was not having any valid driving license on the date of accident for which he as further penalized under Section 3/181 MV Act. The site plan was prepared, and the statement of Sh. Kunal, who had removed the injured to the hospital, was recorded. Statements of other witnesses who were directly or indirectly connected with the accident were also recorded. The nature of injuries sustained MACT No. 01/2021 Shankar Vs Deepak & Ors. Page No. 3 of 27 (rpt) by the injured was opined to be grievous. The Detailed Accident Report (DAR) was also filed by the IO. 3. WRITTEN STATEMENT/REPLY: (a) A joint Written Statement/Reply was filed on behalf of Respondent No. 1 (the driver) and Respondent No. 2 (the owner), wherein they contended that they have been falsely implicated in the present case. It was asserted that no accident occurred due to any rash or negligent driving on the part of Respondent No. 1. On the contrary, it was alleged that the injured himself was negligent, as he suddenly jumped from the left side of the road and came in front of the motorcycle. Consequently, when Respondent No. 1 applied sudden brakes, he lost balance and the motorcycle collided with the injured. (b) A Reply/Written Statement was also filed on behalf of the Insurance Company, wherein a statutory defence was raised to the effect that the driver of the offending vehicle was not holding a valid and effective driving licence at the time of the alleged accident. It was further pointed out that relevant provisions regarding driving without a valid licence were added in the charge sheet. It was contended that it is the bounden duty of the owner to ensure, before handing over the offending vehicle, that the driver possesses a valid driving licence, and that Respondent MACT No. 01/2021 Shankar Vs Deepak & Ors. Page No. 4 of 27 (rpt) Nos. 1 and 2 wilfully committed a breach of the terms and conditions of the insurance policy. Accordingly, it was prayed that the Insurance Company be exonerated from liability. It was further stated that the claimant himself contributed to the accident, as he attempted to cross a busy Ring Road, where high- speed traffic normally passes, despite the presence of a nearby foot overbridge, thereby putting his life in peril. 4. ISSUES : (a) From the pleadings of parties, following issues were framed vide order dated 12.04.2021: i). (a). The matter was thereafter listed for evidence. However, the record reflects that despite several opportunities granted by the Tribunal, the claimant and his counsel failed to take any steps to lead evidence. Consequently, the matter remained pending from the date of framing of issues, i.e., 12.04.2021, till 10.08.2023. In the interim, the Tribunal also closed the interest on the award. Ultimately, vide order dated 10.08.2023, the opportunity to lead evidence on behalf of the claimant was closed, and the matter was thereafter listed for evidence on behalf of the respondents. (b) Driver / R-1/ Deepak Kumar tendered his evidentiary affidavit as Ex.R1W1/A and relied upon his MLC and discharge summary as Ex.R1W1/1 and Ex.R1W1/2 respectively. He was also cross examined on behalf of counsel for claimant. (c) R-2/owner / Akash did not lead any evidence. Ms. Lalita Anand / Administrative Officer of The Oriental Insurance Company Limited tendered her evidentiary affidavit as Ex.R3W1/1 and relied upon copy of insurance policy as Ex.R3W1/2, notice under Order 12 Rule 8 CPC along with postal receipts as Ex.R3W1/3 (colly). (e) Respondent Evidence was then closed. Matter was thereafter listed for Final Arguments. ( a) Final Arguments were advanced by all the contesting parties. (b) Learned counsel for the claimant argued that the accident occurred solely due to the rash and negligent driving of the driver of the offending vehicle, who struck the injured while driving at a high speed and in a negligent manner. It was contended that as a result of the accidental injuries, the claimant suffered immense pain and suffering, as well as financial loss. It was further argued that the injuries rendered the claimant incapacitated from performing any job and that he continues to face difficulty even in carrying out basic routine activities. Accordingly, it was prayed that the injured be awarded just and fair compensation on the basis of the material available on record, including the DAR. He argued that no such accident took place due to rash and negligent driving of driver of offending vehicle rather it was Shankar Kumar (Dar) vs Deepak Kumar (215/20Ln) on 23 December, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/180549015/ 4 injured himself who was negligent in his manner and his negligence was the sole cause of this accident. It is also contended that claimant side has not lead any evidence to substantiate his claim rather driver/ R-1 examined himself in witness box and narrated the whole story and gave true details of accident. It is further argued that claimant has failed to discharge it primary burden of proof since he failed to lead evidence and even any supporting documents about any loss of income and expenditure upon treatment has also not been filed. It is concluded with request that present claim petition be dismissed. (d) Final arguments were also advanced on behalf of the Insurance Company. Learned counsel for the Insurance Company pointed out a breach of the insurance policy on the ground that the driver of the offending vehicle was not holding a valid and effective driving licence at the time of the accident.

Sec. 168 MV Act enjoins the Claim Tribunals to hold an enquiry into the claim to make an effort determining the amount of compensation which appears to it to be just and reasonable. "(1) Award of the Claims Tribunal.--On receipt of an application for compensation made under section 166, the Claims Tribunal shall, after giving notice of the application to the insurer and after giving the parties (including the insurer) an opportunity of being heard, hold an inquiry into the claim or, as the case may be, each of the claims and, subject to the provisions of section 162 may make an award determining the amount of compensation which appears to it to be just and specifying the person or persons to whom compensation shall be paid and in making the award the Claims Tribunal shall specify the amount which shall be paid by the insurer or owner or driver of the vehicle involved in the accident or by all or any of them, as the case may be: Provided that where such application makes a claim for compensation under section 140 in respect of the death or permanent disablement of any person, such claim and any other claim (whether made in such application or otherwise) for compensation in respect of such death or permanent disablement shall be disposed of in accordance with the provisions of Chapter X. (2) The Claims Tribunal shall arrange to deliver copies of the award to the parties concerned expeditiously and in any case within a period of fifteen days from the date of the award. (3) When an award is made under this section, the person who is required to pay any amount in terms of such award shall, within thirty days of the date of announcing the award by the Claims Tribunal, deposit the entire amount awarded in such manner as the Claims Tribunal may direct." The observation of Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Divisional Controller, KSRTC v. Mahadeva Shetty and Another, (2003) 7 SCC 197, needs mention here (para 15): Statutory provisions clearly indicate that the compensation must be "just" and it cannot be a bonanza; not a source of profit but the same should not be a pittance. The courts and tribunals have a duty to weigh the various factors and quantify the amount of compensation, which should be just. What would be "just" compensation is a vexed question. There can be no golden rule applicable to all cases for measuring the value of human life or a limb. Measure of damages cannot be arrived at by precise mathematical calculations. It would depend upon the particular facts and circumstances, and attending peculiar or special features, if any. Every method or mode adopted for assessing compensation has to be considered in the background of "just" compensation which is the pivotal consideration. Though by use of the expression "which appears to it to be just", a wide discretion is vested in the Tribunal, the determination has to be rational, to be done by a judicious approach and not the outcome of whims, wild guesses and arbitrariness.. ..." 12. Delineating the damages as pecuniary and non pecuniary, Hon'ble Supreme Court of India, in case of R. D. Hattangadi Vs. Pest Control (India) Pvt Ltd, 1995 AIR 755, made following MACT No. 01/2021 Shankar Vs Deepak & Ors. Page No. 16 of 27 (rpt) observations: "9....while fixing an amount of compensation payable to a victim of an accident, the damages have to be assessed separately as pecuniary damages and special damages. Pecuniary damages are those which the victim has actually incurred and which are capable of being calculated in terms of money; whereas non-pecuniary damages are those which are incapable of being assessed by arithmetical calculations. In order to appreciate two concepts pecuniary damages may include expenses incurred by the claimant: (i) medical attendance; (ii) loss of earning of profit up to the date of trial; (iii) other material loss. So far non- pecuniary damages are concerned, they may include (i) damages for mental and physical shock, pain and suffering, already suffered or likely to be suffered in future; (ii) damages to compensate for the loss of amenities of life which may include a variety of matters i.e. on account of injury the claimant may not be able to walk, run or sit; (iii) damages for the loss of expectation of life, i.e., on account of injury the normal longevity of the person concerned is shortened; (iv) inconvenience, hardship, discomfort, disappointment, frustration and mental stress in life." The object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner. This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned. [See C.K. Subramania Iyer v. T. Kunhikuttan Nair [(1969) 3 SCC 64 : AIR 1970 SC 376] , R.D. Hattangadi v. Pest Control (India) (P) Ltd. [(1995) 1 SCC 551 : 1995 SCC (Cri) 250] and Baker v. Willoughby [1970 AC 467 : (1970) 2 WLR 50 : (1969) 3 All ER 1528 (HL)] .] 6. The heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following: Pecuniary damages (Special damages) (i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalisation, medicines, transportation, nourishing food, and miscellaneous expenditure. (ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising: (a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment; (b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability. (iii) Future medical expenses. This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life, his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned. [See C.K. Subramania Iyer v. T. Kunhikuttan Nair [(1969) 3 SCC 64 : AIR 1970 SC 376] , R.D. Hattangadi v. Pest Control (India) (P) Ltd. [(1995) 1 SCC 551 : 1995 SCC (Cri) 250] and Baker v. Willoughby [1970 AC 467 : (1970) 2 WLR 50 : (1969) 3 All ER 1528 (HL)] .] 6. The heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following: Pecuniary damages (Special damages) (i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalisation, medicines, transportation, nourishing food, and miscellaneous expenditure. (ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising: (a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment; (b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability. (iii) Future medical expenses. (v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage). The abovesaid principles have been placed reliance upon in a recent judgment reported as Sidram Vs. The Divisional Manager United India Insurance Co. Ltd and Anr., arising out of SLP (Civil) no. 19277 of 2018 passed by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India as decided on 16.11.2022. 15. It is settled proposition of law as held in catena of judgments that "just compensation" should include all elements that would go to place the victim in as near a position as she or he was in, before the occurrence of the accident. Whilst no amount of money or other material compensation can erase the trauma, pain and suffering that a victim undergoes after a serious accident, (or replace the loss of a loved one), monetary compensation is the manner known to law, whereby society assures some measure of restitution to those who survive, and the victims who have to face their lives.
